extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, artists, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for choosing subjects and modes of expression in sculpture and painting, and for evaluating the artistic appropriateness (beauty, character, Idea vs. concept, allegory, symbolism, mannerism). Emphasises medium-appropriateness, inward significance, and origins of genuine art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of expression to the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of an effect must lie within the province of the art-medium; if the essential effect depends on another medium (e.g., sound), it ought not to be represented in a medium unable to produce that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in sculpture a shrieking Laocoon 'could not be produced in marble' since the essence of shrieking 'lies entirely in sound' — representing the distorted mouth would sacrifice other expressive features and produce the spectacle of a continuous effort without effect (anti-pattern: depicting a mouth distorted as if to shriek in marble). By contrast, poetry and acting (theatrical performance) may and should represent shrieking, because they can produce the required effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must serve their end (avoid representing means without effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not represent the medium or means of an action when the end/effect cannot be conveyed by the work; representing the means alone (without the end) is absurd and ridicules the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a sculptured figure with a mouth distorted as if to shriek but incapable of producing sound creates a 'continuous effort without effect' (compared to stuffing a horn and watching vain attempts to blow it). The means chosen must actually achieve the intended perceptual effect in that medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture's preference for nakedness and use of drapery
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty accompanied by grace is the principal object of sculpture; it loves nakedness and allows clothing only so far as it does not conceal the form. Drapery should be used not as covering but as a means of exhibiting the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drapery functions like foreshortening in painting: a suggestion that forces the understanding to perceive the underlying form. Use drapery only to reveal and suggest the body's form; avoid concealing or confusing the perception of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting secondary activities must not demand violent distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: When painting actions such as playing music, depiction is permissible if it 'demands no violent movement of the body, or distortion of the mouth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable examples: St. Cecilia at the organ, Raphael’s violin-player. Anti-pattern: depicting activities that require unnatural contortions which would harm the overall beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical painting's principal aims: beauty, grace, and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical painting should pursue beauty and grace but above all character — the representation of will at the highest grade of its objectification, making the Idea of man visible in bearing, occupation, and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the problem of historical painting by placing before the viewer scenes and representative individuals that manifest the Idea; use actions and arranged circumstances to disclose peculiar characteristics and inward significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art concerns inward significance, not outward historical importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of art is the inward significance — the depth of insight into the Idea of man — rather than the outward importance of an event in historical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A seemingly mundane scene can possess great inward significance if it reveals human nature; conversely, an event of great historical consequence may be artistically ordinary if it reveals nothing inwardly significant. Example: 'Moses found by the Egyptian princess' has nominal historical significance, but the real given to the onlooker is the perceptible scene of a foundling rescued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects whose chief point is perceptibly representable
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those historical subjects should be chosen the chief point of which can actually be represented perceptibly; avoid subjects whose significance must be reached only by thought (nominal significance too remote from real significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chief incident is offstage or can only be inferred (as in some French tragedy conventions), that is a fault in pictorial art because the real significance must be perceptible, not merely thought about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select pictorially rich subjects (avoid poor pictorial fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical subjects are disadvantageous when they confine the artist to a field chosen for non-artistic reasons and poor in picturesque and significant objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism: certain scriptural or narrowly local histories may provide miserable material for pictorial treatment; choose subjects that afford varied, significant, and pictorially interesting circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ethical representation: depiction of inward spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures that reveal the ethical or spiritual spirit (e.g., groups of saints with expressions of completed knowledge and resignation) can represent the highest achievements of painting, even when they do not depict events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such works are not properly 'historical' in the outward sense but succeed by making spiritual knowledge perceptible in faces and bearing. Examples: early Raphael and Correggio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art must represent the Idea (not the concept or the particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of art is an Idea (in Plato’s sense): a determinate, perceptible unity that is neither the mere particular thing nor the abstract concept. The Idea is the source of genuine art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine works spring from direct apprehension of life by the artist (the Idea), not from abstract concepts; the artist works from feeling and unconscious inspiration rather than from an abstract justification. Imitators who start from concepts produce barren, mannered works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting artistic production from concepts (avoid mannerism/imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators and mannerists start from concepts: they observe effects in true works, fix them in concepts, and then imitate dexterously but without inner life. Such works are barren in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mannerism is an anti-pattern: works that are merely collections of recognizable parts (like a machine mincing inputs) lack the assimilating, creative life of genius. Mannered work is age-bound and soon becomes insipid; true works are drawn from nature and life and endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory is inappropriate in plastic and pictorial art
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegory (a work of art that means something different from what it represents) is a mistaken effort in plastic and pictorial art because it draws the mind away from the perceptible Idea to an abstract conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory reduces pictorial art to 'hieroglyphics' — if an allegorical picture has artistic value, that value is separate from and independent of its allegorical meaning. Examples of weak allegory: forced symbolic devices (tortoise for feminine seclusion, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish allegory's role in poetry vs visual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory and tropes are permissible and often serviceable in poetry because poetry starts from concept and uses language to lead the imagination to perceptions; in visual art the relation is reversed and allegory misleads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allegory, metaphor, parable in literary genres; examples of effective poetic/figurative allegory: Cervantes, Kleist, Homer, Plato's cave, Menenius Agrippa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conventional symbolism and emblems in pictorial art
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional symbols (rose = secrecy, laurel = fame, etc.) and emblems are mere hieroglyphics and their value is foreign to true art; they signify by convention rather than by perceptible Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat emblems and heraldic/symbolic devices as external to the end of art; where such signs are used, the pictorial/artistic value should be judged independently of their emblematic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic value must not be subordinated to serving another end
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that attempt to serve two ends (e.g., a statue that is also a candelabrum, or an allegory intended primarily as a legend) compromise the proper end of art — representation of a perceivable Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True lovers of art will not accept works primarily serving utilitarian or didactic-hieroglyphic ends; any secondary function must not intrude on the perceptible artistic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simplicity of expression (general stylistic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those possessing a rich mind express themselves in the most natural, direct, and simple way; poverty of mind cloaks itself in far-fetched, obscure, and pompous phraseology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to artists/writers: favour natural, direct expression over ornate obscurity. Anti-pattern: obscuring small or commonplace thoughts under 'barbaric finery' or pompous phrase.
